Added reducing sugars help where the food is protein-rich but sugar-poor, which is the logic behind a pinch of sugar or a brush of milk or honey. Higher fat content aids browning by conducting heat well and by exceeding 100 degrees where water cannot.

The counterpart is acrylamide, formed from asparagine and reducing sugars above about 120 degrees in starchy foods. Current advice is to aim for golden rather than dark brown on potatoes, bread and other starches — a genuine, if modest, reason not to push browning to its limit.

sections.heading: Carryover, Gradients and Why Resting Works
sections.body:
Take a roast from the oven and its temperature does not stop rising. The surface may be at 150 degrees, the layer beneath at 90, and the centre at 55. Heat flows down a gradient, and that gradient does not vanish because the oven door closed. Energy stored in the hot outer layers continues to flow inward while the surface simultaneously loses heat to the room, and the centre temperature keeps climbing for some minutes before it peaks and begins to fall.

This is carryover cooking, and its magnitude scales with the steepness of the gradient and the size of the object. A thin steak seared hard may carry over 2 to 4 degrees. A 2 kilogram roast at 190 degrees oven temperature commonly carries over 5 to 8 degrees. A large turkey or a whole suckling pig can carry over 10 degrees or more. A joint cooked low and slow at 120 degrees has a much shallower gradient and may carry over barely 1 to 2 degrees.

The practical rule is to remove meat from the heat below its target and let carryover finish the job, and the amount of undershoot must be judged from the size of the piece and the harshness of the cooking temperature — not from a single number applied to everything. Removing a roast at 52 to 54 degrees for a medium-rare finish near 57 to 60 is typical; removing a thin steak at that temperature would leave it under.

Resting does a second thing that is genuinely about heat transfer, though it is usually explained in terms of juices. During resting the internal gradient flattens by conduction: the outer layers give up energy to the interior and to the air until the piece approaches uniformity. A joint sliced immediately shows a broad grey band beneath a dark crust and a narrow pink core; the same joint rested twenty minutes shows a far more even colour, because the gradient itself has relaxed.

The juice argument is partly true and often overstated. Muscle proteins denature and contract with heat, squeezing water out of the fibres into the spaces between them; as the meat cools those proteins relax slightly and the extruded liquid is partly reabsorbed and made more viscous. Measurements do show reduced purge from rested meat, though the effect is smaller than the folklore claims. The honest summary is that resting flattens the temperature gradient reliably and reduces immediate juice loss modestly.

A related consequence concerns the widespread advice to bring meat to room temperature before cooking. Because meat's thermal diffusivity is so low, a thick roast sitting on the counter for an hour warms perhaps 2 to 3 degrees at the centre while its surface sits in the bacterial danger zone. The effect on cooking time is small enough to be within the noise of oven variation, and the food safety cost is real. The practice is largely theatre; a longer rest after cooking does far more.

sections.heading: Measuring Heat: Thermometers, Placement and Thermal Lag
sections.body:
Every claim in this field collapses without measurement, because human perception of temperature is unreliable above about 60 degrees and non-existent inside a piece of meat. A thermometer is the instrument that converts cooking from ritual into control, and choosing and using one well is a skill in itself.

Three sensor technologies dominate. Thermocouples exploit the Seebeck effect — a voltage generated at the junction of two dissimilar metals — and because the junction can be made vanishingly small, they respond in well under a second and can be built into a needle probe fine enough not to leak juice. Thermistors are semiconductors whose resistance changes steeply with temperature; they are accurate, inexpensive and typically respond in two to six seconds. Bimetallic dial thermometers work by the differential expansion of two bonded metals coiled into a spring, are slow at fifteen to thirty seconds, and — critically — sense along a substantial length of the stem rather than at the tip, so they average over five centimetres or more and are useless in anything thin.

Placement dominates accuracy. The reading you want is the coldest point, which in a symmetrical joint is the geometric centre, but in a bird is the deepest part of the thigh next to but not touching the bone, and in an irregular piece is wherever the mass is thickest. Bone conducts differently from muscle and a probe touching it reads high. A probe in a pocket of fat reads differently from one in muscle. The reliable technique is to push the probe through until it clearly passes the centre and then withdraw slowly, watching for the minimum reading — the temperature will fall, bottom out and rise again, and the bottom is the centre.

Thermal lag is the trap that catches even careful cooks. A probe has its own mass and must come to equilibrium with its surroundings; a cold probe inserted into hot food initially reads low and climbs. Waiting for the reading to stabilise is not optional. It is also why an instant-read used to check a pan surface will read low if simply touched to the metal for a moment.

Infrared thermometers are excellent for surfaces and useless for interiors. They measure emitted radiation and infer temperature, which means they are sensitive to emissivity: a shiny stainless pan or a polished aluminium sheet may read 50 degrees or more below its true temperature because it emits so little. They are ideal for checking oil, a cast iron surface, or a pizza stone, provided the surface is dark and matt.

For calibration, ice water should read 0 degrees Celsius and vigorously boiling water 100 at sea level, less at altitude. Checking both points takes two minutes and reveals a surprising number of faulty instruments straight out of the box.

sections.heading: Microwaves: Heating Without Heat Transfer
sections.body:
A microwave oven does not transfer heat in the ordinary sense at all. It generates electromagnetic radiation at 2.45 gigahertz — a wavelength of about 12.2 centimetres — from a magnetron, and floods the cavity with a standing wave pattern. Water molecules are electrically polar, with a slight negative charge at the oxygen and positive charges at the hydrogens, so an oscillating electric field torques them back and forth roughly two and a half billion times a second. Friction between the tumbling molecules and their neighbours turns that motion into thermal energy. Fats and sugars respond too, though less strongly; ice responds very weakly because its molecules are locked in a lattice and cannot rotate freely.

This dielectric heating deposits energy in a volume rather than at a surface, which is genuinely different from conduction, convection and radiation. But the popular claim that microwaves cook from the inside out is wrong. Penetration depth in moist food at this frequency is only about 1 to 3 centimetres, beyond which the field is substantially attenuated. Anything thicker is still heated at its outer layers and relies on conduction inward, exactly like conventional cooking. The apparent inside-out effect in a jacket potato comes from the skin losing heat to the cool cavity air while the interior does not.

Two consequences shape practice. Uneven heating is intrinsic, because the standing wave has nodes and antinodes and because different components of a dish absorb differently. Turntables and stirrer fans mitigate but do not eliminate this, so stirring partway through and allowing a standing time of one to three minutes for conduction to even out the gradient are both genuinely necessary, not manufacturer caution. Reheating meat or rice to a safe temperature throughout, in particular, cannot be assumed from a hot exterior.

Second, the ice anomaly means defrosting is awkward: the first patch to melt absorbs energy far better than the surrounding ice and races ahead, cooking while its neighbours are still frozen. Defrost settings work by pulsing the magnetron at low duty cycle, giving conduction time to even things out between bursts.

The physics also imposes a ceiling. Because energy goes into water and water boils at 100 degrees, a microwaved food surface rarely exceeds that and therefore does not brown or crisp. Combination appliances add a grill element or hot air precisely to supply the surface radiation the microwave cannot.

Superheating is the real safety hazard. Water in a smooth container with no nucleation sites can exceed 100 degrees without boiling, then flash-boil violently when disturbed. Placing a wooden stirrer or a rough-surfaced object in the cup, and letting it stand thirty seconds before removal, avoids this.

sections.heading: Equilibrium Cooking: Sous Vide, Low and Slow, and the Reverse Sear
sections.body:
Conventional cooking runs a race between the surface, which is overcooking, and the centre, which is not yet done. Equilibrium cooking removes the race by holding the food in an environment at the target temperature itself, so no part can exceed it however long it stays.

Sous vide is the pure form: food is sealed in a bag and immersed in water held within a fraction of a degree by a circulator whose forced convection prevents cold pockets. Because water's convective coefficient is hundreds of times that of still air, the food reaches bath temperature quickly and then simply stays there. The safety logic is that pasteurisation is a rate process rather than a threshold — a 7-log reduction of Salmonella in chicken takes essentially no time at 74 degrees, about 4 minutes at 65, roughly 35 minutes at 60 — so low temperatures are safe provided the time is right.

Low-and-slow barbecue and low-oven roasting are the same idea applied loosely. At an oven setting of 105 to 120 degrees the gradient between surface and centre is shallow, so the outer layers are only a few degrees ahead of the middle and the whole piece finishes nearly uniform. It is also why the barbecue stall happens: as the surface saturates with rendered moisture, evaporation at 2,257 kilojoules per kilogram exactly balances the incoming energy and the internal temperature plateaus for hours near 65 to 70 degrees. Wrapping in foil or paper stops the evaporation and the temperature resumes climbing at once, which is the whole mechanism behind the Texas crutch.

The trade-off is that nothing browns, since no part of the food ever exceeds the bath temperature. The crust must be added separately, in a deliberately brief high-temperature step.
steps: Salt the meat 40 minutes to 24 hours ahead so surface moisture is drawn out and reabsorbed, leaving a drier exterior that browns fast later.

For a reverse sear, cook in an oven at 105 to 135 degrees Celsius, or in a water bath at the exact finish temperature, until the centre is 3 to 5 degrees below target. The shallow gradient means carryover will be small.
Measure at the geometric centre with a fast probe, withdrawing slowly to find the minimum reading rather than trusting a single insertion.
Rest the piece uncovered for 10 minutes and pat the surface bone dry. Any surface water will consume the sear pan's energy on evaporation instead of browning.
Preheat a heavy cast iron or carbon steel pan until a flicked water droplet skitters rather than spreads, indicating a surface above roughly 190 degrees Celsius.
Add a thin film of a high smoke point oil and sear 45 to 90 seconds per face, pressing for full contact. The goal is maximum surface temperature for minimum time, so the browned layer stays thin.
Finish edges and fat cap by holding the piece on its side with tongs, then remove immediately. A blowtorch is an acceptable alternative and deposits even less heat inward.
Slice at once. A reverse-seared piece has already rested, so a second long rest only cools it.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: Diagnosing What Went Wrong
sections.body:
Most cooking failures are heat transfer failures with recognisable signatures, and learning to read the signature is faster than trial and error.

Grey band under the crust, correct centre. The surface energy was applied for too long, so the browning front had time to conduct inward. The fix is a hotter, briefer sear, a drier surface, or separating browning from cooking entirely with a reverse sear.

Pale and steamed rather than browned. The surface never dried, so it never exceeded 100 degrees. Causes are a wet surface, a crowded pan, a pan with too little thermal mass to survive contact with cold food, or a heat source too weak for the load. Cook in batches, dry the food, use a heavier pan.

Burnt outside, raw inside. The gradient was too steep for the thickness. Because penetration time scales with the square of thickness, a thick piece simply cannot be rushed. Lower the temperature and extend the time, or start with gentle heat and brown at the end.

Burnt bottom, pale top in baking. Unequal mechanisms: conduction from a dark sheet or a hot stone is outrunning radiation from above. Move the rack up, use a lighter-coloured or doubled sheet, or lower the oven floor heat.

Sauce breaking or scorching in a stainless pan. Poor conductivity means a hot ring over the burner. Use a clad or heavy pan, stir to thin the boundary layer, and lower the flame — reaction rate roughly doubles per 10 degree rise, so a modest reduction buys a large margin.

Greasy fried food. Oil below about 160 degrees produced too little steam to keep oil out, or the batch was too large and crashed the temperature. Recover between batches, drain immediately while hot.

Custard curdling or eggs scrambling in a sauce. The pan surface, not the bulk liquid, is what the eggs feel, and a thin pan over a strong flame holds its base far above the sauce it contains. Egg proteins set near 62 to 65 degrees and seize above about 82. Use a heavy pan, a bain-marie or a diffuser.

Uneven microwave reheating. Penetration depth is only 1 to 3 centimetres and the cavity holds a standing wave with cold nodes. Stir midway, arrange food in a ring, and allow standing time.

Roast done too early or too late against the recipe. Weight-based timings are unreliable because shape, not mass, sets the conduction distance, and because domestic ovens commonly run 10 to 25 degrees off their dial. Cook to internal temperature, not to the clock.

Two honest limits are worth stating. First, most of the coefficients used here — the convective h values, the effective diffusivity of a real piece of meat — are approximations that vary with geometry, surface roughness, moisture and airflow, and no domestic calculation should be treated as precise. Second, predictive models and published time-temperature tables are built on idealised, uniform samples; a real bird with a bone, a fat cap and an air cavity behaves less tidily. Measurement at the coldest point, every time, is the only thing that removes the uncertainty.

guides.safetyNote: Hot fat and steam cause the most serious kitchen burns. Steam at 100 degrees Celsius releases about 2,257 kilojoules per kilogram as it condenses on skin, so it scalds far worse than boiling water — always open lids and oven doors away from your face and hands. Never add water to hot oil or move a burning pan; smother a fat fire by cutting the heat and covering it, and never use water on it. Water heated in a smooth microwave-safe container can superheat above 100 degrees and flash-boil when disturbed, so let it stand before removing it. Low-temperature and sous-vide cooking is safe only when the correct time is held at the correct temperature; do not shorten a hold to save time, and cool and refrigerate promptly anything not eaten straight away.

guides.title: Induction Cooking: How the Field Heats Steel
guides.summary: How an induction hob turns a magnetic field into heat inside the pan itself — eddy currents, hysteresis, skin depth and the power electronics that make it work — and what that physics means in practice for cookware choice, technique, efficiency, installation and troubleshooting.

sections.heading: What Induction Is, and Why the Distinction Matters
sections.body:
An induction hob does something that no other cooking appliance does: it makes the pan itself the
heating element. There is no flame, no glowing coil, no hot plate underneath transferring energy
upward. Beneath the ceramic glass sits a flat spiral of copper wire carrying a rapidly alternating
current, and that current generates a rapidly alternating magnetic field which passes straight
through the glass — glass being magnetically transparent — and into the base of the pan sitting on
it. In the metal of the pan that changing field drives swirling electrical currents and, in
ferromagnetic materials, repeated flipping of magnetic domains. Both processes dissipate energy as
heat, in the pan, exactly where the food is. The glass surface is never directly heated at all; it
gets warm only because a hot pan is sitting on it.

That single architectural difference cascades into most of what people notice about induction. The
response is fast, because there is no thermal mass of a burner or element that has to heat up and
cool down; changing the power setting changes the current in the coil within milliseconds and the
pan's temperature follows within a second or two, which is a directness gas cannot match and radiant
electric cannot approach. The efficiency is high, because very little energy goes anywhere except
into the pan. The surface is comparatively safe: spilled sugar does not carbonise onto a red-hot
element, a tea towel dropped on an idle zone does not ignite, and the residual heat that does exist
is conducted back from the pan rather than stored in the appliance. And a kitchen with induction is
markedly cooler and quieter in terms of combustion, since there is no flue gas, no water vapour and
no carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide or fine particulate being released into the room.

The trade is that the pan must be able to participate. A material that will not carry substantial
eddy currents or does not have magnetic domains to flip cannot be heated this way, which rules out
plain aluminium, copper, glass, and most non-magnetic stainless alloys unless they have been
deliberately built with a ferrous layer. This is the single most common source of frustration for
new users and it is entirely a materials-physics constraint rather than a manufacturer's whim.

Induction is not new. Patents for induction cooking appear from the 1900s, a working range was
demonstrated at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, and Westinghouse built a prototype called the Cool Top
in the 1950s. What made it a mass-market product was the semiconductor: cheap, robust, fast
high-power switching transistors capable of chopping mains electricity into tens of kilohertz did not
become economic until the 1980s and 1990s. Induction is therefore best understood as
nineteenth-century physics waiting for late-twentieth-century power electronics.

sections.heading: Faraday's Law: The Physics the Whole Appliance Rests On
sections.body:
The governing principle was discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831 and independently by Joseph Henry
at almost the same time. Faraday found that moving a magnet through a coil of wire produced a
current, and, more generally, that a changing magnetic field through any conducting loop drives an
electromotive force around that loop. The relationship is written as Faraday's law of induction: the
induced electromotive force equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit,
or in symbols, EMF equals minus d-phi-by-d-t. The minus sign is Lenz's law, stated by Heinrich Lenz
in 1834, which says the induced current always flows in whichever direction opposes the change that
created it. Lenz's law is why an induction hob feels a pan as an electrical load at all and why the
appliance can detect whether a pan is present.

The two words that carry the weight are changing and rate. A static magnetic field, however strong,
induces nothing; a fridge magnet next to a saucepan does nothing at all. What matters is how fast the
flux changes. Double the frequency and, for the same peak field, you double the rate of change and
therefore double the induced voltage, which for a given resistance quadruples the power dissipated.
This is why induction hobs run at 20 to 100 kilohertz rather than at the 50 or 60 hertz of the mains
supply: at mains frequency the induced currents would be feeble, and you would need an impractically
large field to heat anything. Operating above about 20 kilohertz also has the virtue of pushing the
fundamental switching frequency above the upper limit of adult human hearing, though harmonics and
mechanical resonances still produce the audible hum many users notice.

The magnetic field itself is produced by the coil according to Ampère's law, elaborated by James
Clerk Maxwell into the set of four equations published in 1865 that unify electricity and magnetism.
A current flowing in a loop of wire creates a magnetic field threading through it; a flat spiral of
many turns creates a field that emerges from the centre, arcs outward and returns, and any conductor
placed in that returning flux experiences the changing field. In a well-designed hob the coil is
backed by ferrite bars — a ceramic magnetic material — which shape the field upward toward the pan
and reduce stray field leaking downward into the electronics and the countertop.

The elegance is that the coupling between coil and pan is exactly that of a transformer with a
single-turn, short-circuited secondary winding. The pan is the secondary. It is a transformer whose
secondary is deliberately made lossy, so that all the power delivered into it appears as heat rather
than as usable current.

sections.heading: Eddy Currents and Joule Heating: The Primary Mechanism
sections.body:
When the alternating field penetrates the base of a pan, it induces electromotive force not around a
tidy wire loop but throughout the bulk of the metal. Because the metal is a continuous conductor,
that electromotive force drives closed circular currents swirling within the material, called eddy
currents after the analogy with water. They were first characterised by Léon Foucault in 1855, which
is why they are sometimes called Foucault currents.

Those currents encounter the electrical resistance of the metal, and resistance converts electrical
energy into heat. This is Joule heating, named for James Prescott Joule, and its magnitude is given
by the relation that power equals current squared times resistance. The squaring is important: it
means the heating is very sensitive to how strongly the currents are driven, and a modest increase in
field strength or frequency produces a large increase in power. In a domestic hob the induced current
in the pan base can be on the order of hundreds of amperes circulating in a very low-resistance
sheet, and the whole of that is dissipated as heat within a layer only fractions of a millimetre
thick.

Two material properties decide how effective this is, and they pull in opposite directions in a way
that is initially counter-intuitive. High electrical conductivity means large induced currents, but
it also means very low resistance, so the current-squared-times-resistance product can end up small;
and high conductivity confines the currents into a very thin surface layer. Copper and aluminium are
superb conductors and are, for this reason, poor induction targets at ordinary hob frequencies —
their resistivity is so low that the coupled resistance seen by the coil is a fraction of an ohm, too
low for the inverter to drive efficiently. Steel, by contrast, has roughly six times the resistivity
of aluminium, and magnetic stainless grades higher still, so the induced currents meet meaningful
resistance and deposit their energy readily.

The heat therefore appears not in the food, not in the glass, and not evenly through the pan, but in
a thin annular band in the base of the pan directly above the coil windings. It then spreads by
ordinary conduction through the base and up the walls. This is why the thickness and conductivity of
the pan base matters enormously for evenness: a thin steel pan will develop a visible ring pattern
matching the coil, scorching a pancake in a doughnut shape, whereas a pan with a thick aluminium or
copper core sandwiched behind a steel outer layer will smear that heat laterally within a second or
two and cook evenly. The best induction cookware is therefore a composite that separates the two
jobs: a ferrous layer to absorb the field, and a highly conductive layer to spread the resulting
heat.

sections.heading: Hysteresis: The Second Heating Mechanism and Why Iron Is Special
sections.body:
Eddy currents are not the whole story. In a ferromagnetic material — iron, nickel, cobalt, and alloys
containing enough of them — there is a second, independent heating process called hysteresis loss,
and it explains why a hob is fussy about magnetism rather than merely about metal.

Ferromagnetic materials contain magnetic domains: microscopic regions, typically a few micrometres
across, within which the atomic magnetic moments are already aligned with one another. In an
unmagnetised piece of iron these domains point in random directions and cancel out. Apply an external
magnetic field and the domains whose alignment matches the field grow at the expense of their
neighbours, the domain walls sweeping through the crystal, and eventually the remaining domains
rotate to align. Reverse the field and the whole rearrangement must happen again in the opposite
direction. Because domain walls snag on grain boundaries, impurities and dislocations in the crystal
lattice, this rearrangement is not reversible without loss; energy is expended overcoming that
friction, and it emerges as heat.

Plot the material's magnetisation against the applied field over a full cycle and you get a loop
rather than a line — the hysteresis loop, the term coined by James Alfred Ewing in 1881 from the
Greek for lagging behind. The area enclosed by that loop is the energy dissipated per cycle per unit
volume. Multiply by the frequency and you have the hysteresis power. At 25 kilohertz the material is
being taken around that loop twenty-five thousand times a second, so even a modest loop area produces
substantial heating.

How much of an induction hob's output comes from hysteresis rather than eddy currents is genuinely
debated and depends heavily on the material and the operating point. Common engineering estimates put
hysteresis at somewhere between a tenth and a third of the total in ordinary carbon steel and
magnetic stainless pans, with eddy currents supplying the remainder. Some popular explanations
overstate hysteresis considerably. What is not in dispute is that ferromagnetism helps in a second,
larger way: the high magnetic permeability of iron concentrates the magnetic flux into the pan base,
raising the local field enormously compared with a non-magnetic material, which in turn drives far
stronger eddy currents. Iron's relative permeability can be several hundred to several thousand,
against essentially one for aluminium and copper.

There is an important temperature limit hiding in this. Every ferromagnetic material has a Curie
temperature above which thermal agitation destroys the domain structure and the material becomes
merely paramagnetic. For iron that point is 770 degrees Celsius, for nickel 358, and for the
magnetic stainless grades used in cookware it is generally in the 600 to 750 range. Ordinary cooking
never approaches this, but industrial induction heating does, and a workpiece heated through its
Curie point shows a sudden drop in coupling and a change in heating rate — a phenomenon exploited
deliberately in some self-regulating induction soldering and brazing tools.

sections.heading: Skin Depth: Why the Heat Lives in a Thin Shell
sections.body:
Alternating currents do not distribute themselves evenly through a conductor. They crowd toward the
surface, an effect called the skin effect, because the changing field inside the conductor induces
counter-currents in the interior that cancel the flow there. The characteristic distance over which
the current density falls to about 37 per cent — one over e — of its surface value is called the skin
depth, and it is one of the most useful numbers in understanding induction heating.

Skin depth is given by the square root of the material's resistivity divided by the product of pi,
the frequency, and the magnetic permeability. Two consequences follow immediately. Higher frequency
means shallower penetration, in inverse proportion to the square root of frequency. And higher
magnetic permeability also means shallower penetration, which is why iron's skin depth is
dramatically smaller than that of a non-magnetic metal of similar resistivity.

The numbers make the design decisions obvious. At 25 kilohertz, the skin depth in carbon steel with a
relative permeability of several hundred is on the order of 0.05 to 0.1 millimetres. In magnetic
stainless steels, with lower permeability and higher resistivity, it is a few tenths of a millimetre.
In aluminium at the same frequency it is about 0.5 millimetres, and in copper about 0.4 — but with
resistivity so low that the effective resistance presented to the coil remains tiny. This is the
quantitative reason that an aluminium pan does not heat: not that no current is induced, but that the
current meets so little resistance that almost no power is dissipated, and the coil sees a load it
cannot efficiently drive.

The shallowness of the ferrous skin depth is what makes clad cookware work so well. A stainless steel
outer disc only 0.4 to 0.5 millimetres thick is already several skin depths deep, so essentially all
the field energy is absorbed in that layer and none escapes into the aluminium behind it. The
aluminium then does its job as a lateral heat spreader without ever needing to interact with the
field at all. It also explains why an induction disc adaptor — a thick ferrous plate placed under a
non-magnetic pan — works but performs poorly: the plate heats, but the energy then has to cross a
poor contact interface into the pan above, and much of it radiates away instead.

Skin depth also explains why induction cooktops sit where they do in frequency. Go much below 20
kilohertz and the switching noise becomes audible and the penetration deepens, requiring thicker
pans. Go far above 100 kilohertz and switching losses in the transistors rise steeply while the skin
depth becomes so shallow that surface finish and coating begin to matter. Twenty to fifty kilohertz
is the practical sweet spot for domestic cooking, and most hobs sit between 20 and 30 kilohertz at
full power.

sections.heading: Inside the Hob: Rectifier, Inverter, Coil and Pan Detection
sections.body:
Strip the glass off an induction hob and the layout is consistent across manufacturers. Mains
alternating current arrives at 230 volts and 50 hertz, or 120 or 240 volts at 60 hertz in North
America, and passes first through an electromagnetic interference filter — a network of chokes and
capacitors whose job is to stop the hob's own high-frequency switching noise travelling back into the
household wiring, where it would interfere with radios and other appliances. Next comes a bridge
rectifier and a bulk smoothing capacitor, converting the alternating supply to a direct-current bus
of roughly 325 volts on a 230-volt supply.

That direct-current bus feeds the inverter, which is the heart of the machine. The inverter uses
insulated-gate bipolar transistors, or IGBTs, switching devices capable of handling hundreds of volts
and tens of amperes while turning on and off in well under a microsecond. Most domestic hobs use a
quasi-resonant single-switch topology, in which one IGBT plus a resonant capacitor and the coil itself
form a tuned circuit; more capable and commercial units use half-bridge or full-bridge arrangements
with two or four switches. The controller drives the IGBT at a frequency near the resonance of the
coil-and-capacitor combination, so that the current in the coil swings sinusoidally at tens of
kilohertz with very low switching loss — the transistor turns on when the voltage across it is near
zero, a technique called zero-voltage switching that is essential for keeping the semiconductors cool
enough to survive.

The work coil itself is a flat spiral, typically 140 to 220 millimetres across for a domestic zone,
wound from Litz wire: many fine strands individually insulated and woven so that each strand spends
equal time near the surface and near the centre of the bundle. This defeats the skin effect within
the coil itself, keeping its own resistance low so that it does not waste power heating itself. Behind
the coil sit radial ferrite bars that direct flux upward and shield the electronics below, and beneath
those a temperature sensor, usually a thermistor pressed against the underside of the glass, which
is the hob's only means of knowing anything about how hot the pan is.

Pan detection is a neat trick that falls straight out of Lenz's law. The controller pulses the coil
briefly and measures the resulting current waveform. A suitable ferrous pan on the zone loads the
resonant circuit heavily, changing both the resonant frequency and the damping in a characteristic
way; no pan, or an unsuitable pan, leaves the circuit lightly loaded and ringing. From that
measurement the hob decides whether to deliver power, and it repeats the check continuously, which is
why lifting the pan cuts the power in a fraction of a second and why a pan below the minimum diameter
— usually around 110 to 120 millimetres — is simply ignored.

sections.heading: Which Pans Work: Magnetism, Cladding and the Magnet Test
sections.body:
A pan works on induction if and only if its base couples enough power out of the field, which in
practice means it must contain a substantial ferromagnetic layer at the bottom surface. The
household test is exactly as crude as it sounds and is entirely reliable: hold a refrigerator magnet
against the outside of the base. If it clings firmly, the pan will work. If it falls off or barely
tugs, it will not, or will work so weakly that the hob refuses it.

Cast iron works superbly and couples more strongly than anything else in a normal kitchen; enamelled
cast iron behaves identically, the enamel being only a thin surface glaze. Carbon steel — the
material of a traditional French skillet or a wok — works excellently and heats very fast because its
base is thin. Magnetic stainless steel works, but the phrase requires care:
stainless grades divide by crystal structure. Ferritic grades such as 430 are magnetic and work.
Martensitic grades work. Austenitic grades such as 304, the common 18/8 or 18/10 alloy used for pan
interiors and for cheap single-ply pans, are essentially non-magnetic and do not. This is why a
tri-ply pan is built as 18/10 stainless inside, aluminium core, and a magnetic 430 stainless disc
outside — the outer layer exists purely to talk to the hob.

Plain aluminium, anodised aluminium, copper, titanium, glass, ceramic and most bare non-magnetic
stainless do not work. Many manufacturers bond a ferrous disc to the base of otherwise unsuitable
pans; these function, though a disc smaller than the coil heats unevenly and one that delaminates
rattles.

Two further geometric requirements are easy to overlook. The base must be flat, because coupling
falls off steeply with distance; a warped or convex base sits on a hump and loses a surprising
fraction of its power, and a pan rocking on a domed base will also chatter audibly. And the base must
be large enough to cover a reasonable fraction of the coil, which is why a small espresso pot may not
be recognised on a large zone even though it is made of the right material. Sliding cast iron across
the glass will eventually leave grey metal-transfer marks, which are cosmetic and lift with a
proprietary cream cleaner.
steps: Hold a small refrigerator magnet flat against the centre of the pan's outside base. A firm, hard-to-pull-off grip means good coupling; a weak tug means marginal or no operation.
Repeat the test at the outer edge of the base as well as the centre. A pan with only a small bonded ferrous disc will grip in the middle and release at the rim, and will heat in a small central spot.
Set the pan on the glass and check it does not rock. Press each side in turn; any movement means a warped base and reduced power transfer.
Measure the base diameter and compare it with the minimum stated in the hob's manual, usually 110-120 mm for a standard zone.
Add roughly 500 ml of water and time a full-power boil. A well-matched 2 kW zone reaches a rolling boil in about 90 to 150 seconds; much longer indicates poor coupling.

sections.heading: Power Control: Duty Cycling, True Modulation and the Simmer Problem
sections.body:
An induction zone's power setting is not a valve. There are two quite different ways a hob can
deliver less than full power, and which one your appliance uses determines how it behaves at the low
end, which is where most complaints about induction cooking originate.

The simplest method is duty cycling, sometimes called pulse-width power control at a slow rate. The
inverter runs at full power for part of a repeating cycle and switches off for the rest. Setting five
out of nine on such a hob might mean two seconds on and two seconds off; setting two out of nine
might mean two seconds on and eight seconds off. Averaged over a minute the energy is correct, but
instantaneously the pan is being alternately blasted and left to cool. With a thick pan the thermal
mass smooths this out and nobody notices. With a thin carbon-steel pan or a light saucepan of milk,
the pulsing is clearly audible as a rhythmic click and clearly visible as the sauce alternately
seizing into a boil and subsiding. It is the single most common reason people say induction cannot
simmer.

The better method is genuine continuous modulation, in which the inverter varies the switching
frequency, the duty of the high-frequency switching, or the bus voltage to deliver a smoothly reduced
power without ever ceasing. Because power transfer varies steeply with how far the drive frequency
sits from the resonant peak, shifting the frequency upward from resonance reduces coupling
continuously. Good hobs do this over most of the range and reserve duty cycling only for the very
lowest one or two settings, where the required power is below what the inverter can stably deliver.
Cheaper hobs and most inexpensive portable single-zone units duty-cycle across almost the whole
range. The distinction is rarely stated on a spec sheet, so the practical test is to set a light
saucepan of water to a low setting and listen for a repeating cycle.

Power ratings themselves have their own arithmetic. A typical European domestic zone is rated 1.4 to
2.3 kilowatts, with a boost or power-sharing function taking one zone to 3.0 or 3.7 kilowatts by
borrowing headroom from its neighbour — which is why activating boost on the front-left often caps
the rear-left. A whole four-zone hob may be rated 7.2 kilowatts or more but be internally limited to
less, and many now offer an installer setting to cap total draw for a weaker supply.

A final quirk worth anticipating: because the hob's only temperature information comes from a sensor
under the glass reading conducted heat, its protective thermal cutbacks respond with a lag. A hob run
hard for a long period may quietly reduce power to protect its own electronics, which reads to the
cook as the appliance losing enthusiasm halfway through a long sear.

sections.heading: Efficiency: The Honest Numbers Behind the Marketing
sections.body:
Induction is genuinely the most efficient common cooking technology, but the figures quoted in
advertising deserve unpacking because they measure different things and the comparison is often made
unfairly.

The usual claim is that induction is around 85 to 90 per cent efficient against roughly 70 to 75 per
cent for radiant electric and about 40 per cent for gas. Those numbers describe pan-transfer
efficiency: the fraction of energy entering the appliance that ends up in the cooking vessel. For
induction, careful standardised testing — the US Department of Energy test procedure and the European
EN 60350-2 standard both measure the energy to heat a specified water load — generally returns
figures in the high seventies to mid eighties for real hobs with real pans, somewhat below the
marketing number, with losses in the inverter semiconductors, the coil's own resistance, the cooling
fan, and the imperfect coupling between coil and pan base. Radiant electric loses energy to the glass,
to sideways radiation and to the mass of the element. Gas loses a very large fraction as hot
combustion products flowing around and past the pan, and worse with a small pan on a large burner.

The comparison changes shape if you widen the boundary. A gas burner burns fuel on site at perhaps 40
per cent transfer efficiency but with no generation or transmission loss. Electricity delivered to
the home has already lost energy at the power station and on the grid; on a fossil-heavy grid the
end-to-end primary-energy efficiency of induction may be roughly comparable to gas, whereas on a grid
with substantial renewable, nuclear or hydro generation induction wins decisively. As grids
decarbonise the case strengthens automatically, which is the main policy reason induction is being
promoted in electrification programmes.

There are second-order benefits that rarely appear in the efficiency figure and matter in practice.
Because so little heat escapes the pan, a kitchen with induction requires less air conditioning in
summer, a real cost in commercial kitchens where the extract and make-up air load is substantial.
Because there is no combustion, there is no indoor emission of nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide,
formaldehyde or ultrafine particulate. Research over the last decade, including work published in
2022 estimating that gas stove use is associated with a meaningful share of childhood asthma cases in
homes with gas cooking, has moved this from a marginal consideration to a central one, though the
epidemiology is contested at the margins and ventilation quality is a large confounder.

The efficiency also shows up as speed. Two litres of water from 20 degrees Celsius to boiling
requires about 0.19 kilowatt-hours of energy delivered to the water. On a 3-kilowatt induction zone at
eighty per cent efficiency that is roughly four and a half minutes; on a typical gas burner delivering
similar nominal power at forty per cent, closer to nine.

sections.heading: Cooking on It: What Actually Changes at the Stove
sections.body:
Moving from gas or radiant electric to induction requires unlearning a small number of habits, and
almost all the adjustment concerns the fact that the pan responds immediately rather than lagging.

Preheating is faster than expected and easy to overshoot. An empty or lightly oiled thin pan on a
high setting can reach smoke point in twenty to thirty seconds, whereas on gas the same pan would
take two minutes. The standard error is to set full power, walk away to fetch ingredients, and return
to a scorching pan and burnt oil. The remedy is to preheat at a middling setting and to treat full
power as a deliberate, attended action.

Because there is no flame licking up the sides, heat is concentrated in the base footprint. This is
excellent for searing and for anything where you want the base hot and the walls cool, and it is a
disadvantage for a wok, whose entire geometry assumes a flame wrapping the bowl. Flat-bottomed woks
work reasonably on a standard flat zone but never replicate the sides-hot behaviour; dedicated
concave induction wok hobs, with a bowl-shaped coil, solve this properly and are common in
professional Asian kitchens.

Techniques that rely on lifting the pan away from the heat fail, because power stops the instant the
pan leaves the glass. Tossing food in a pan, flambéing, and the small constant adjustments of angle
that a gas cook makes without thinking all become momentary interruptions of heating. The
compensation is that you can simply change the setting instead, and the change takes effect at once.

Some things become dramatically easier. Holding a precise temperature for a delicate sauce,
chocolate, or a custard is far more controllable than on gas because the response is direct and the
low end of a good hob is genuinely low. Boiling large volumes is fast. Deep-frying at a stable
temperature is more consistent, and many hobs now include a temperature-probe mode or a
built-in oil-temperature setting that closes a control loop using the under-glass sensor. Cleaning is
transformed, because spills land on a surface at perhaps 60 to 80 degrees rather than several hundred
and wipe off rather than carbonising.

Sound and feel take adjustment. The absence of a visible flame removes the cue that tells you a
burner is on, so glancing at the control panel replaces glancing at the flame. Foil, a stainless
trivet or a stray knife on an active zone will all heat, sometimes dangerously fast.

Finally, the pan matters more than it did. On gas, a mediocre pan is partly rescued by the flame
heating the walls. On induction, a thin base with no heat-spreading layer will produce a visible ring
of scorching that matches the coil, and no amount of technique corrects it. Investing in cookware
with a thick aluminium or copper core behind a magnetic outer layer is the single highest-return
change most people can make.

sections.heading: Noise, Vibration and Electromagnetic Interference
sections.body:
Induction hobs make several distinct sounds, and knowing which is normal and which is a symptom saves
a good deal of anxiety.

The most common is a hum or buzz from the pan itself, most noticeable at high power and with
multi-layer clad cookware. It is genuine magnetostriction and Lorentz forcing: the alternating field
makes the ferrous layer physically change dimension very slightly at twice the drive frequency, and
where two bonded layers of different materials are involved they flex against each other. Thin or
poorly bonded pans buzz loudest, cast iron least. A pan that suddenly begins to buzz far more than it
used to may be delaminating.

A second sound is a light, high clicking or ticking at low settings, which is the duty-cycle
switching described in any hob that pulses power at the bottom of its range. It is normal on cheaper
units. A third is fan noise: every induction hob has a cooling fan for the IGBTs and it will run at
high power and continue for several minutes after cooking stops. A fan that never stops, or that runs
loudly at low power, may indicate a blocked air path — most hobs draw air from the front or
underside, and a tightly sealed cabinet installation starves them.

A rattle or vibration usually means a pan with a slightly domed base resonating on the glass, and it
is cured by a different pan or, temporarily, by a little weight in it.

Electromagnetic interference is the other side of the coin. A device switching kilowatts at tens of
kilohertz radiates, and hobs contain substantial filtering to meet the electromagnetic compatibility
limits set by standards such as CISPR 14 and the European EMC Directive. Within those limits, real
interactions still occur. Cheap AM radios near a hob will pick up buzzing. Some induction hobs
interfere with wireless meat thermometers and, historically, with certain hearing aids, though modern
digital aids are much less susceptible. Bank cards, hotel keys and any magnetic-stripe media should
be kept off the surface: the alternating field will corrupt the stripe, and though chip data is
unaffected, the stripe is not recoverable.

The field itself falls off very rapidly with distance because a flat spiral coil is a poor radiator at
these frequencies; the field is largely confined between the coil and the pan. Measurements typically
show the magnetic flux density dropping by more than an order of magnitude within 30 centimetres of
the hob edge. Where a pan is significantly smaller than the coil, or offset from it, more field
escapes at the edge, which is one practical reason to use a correctly sized, correctly centred pan
rather than a small one on a large zone.

sections.heading: Health, Electromagnetic Fields and Implanted Devices
sections.body:
The question people ask most often about induction is whether the field is harmful, and the answer
requires distinguishing between two very different physical regimes that are frequently conflated.

Induction hobs operate at 20 to 100 kilohertz, in what is called the intermediate frequency band.
This is non-ionising radiation: the photon energy is many orders of magnitude too low to break
chemical bonds or damage DNA, unlike X-rays or gamma rays. Nor is it in the microwave band where
tissue heating is the concern; a microwave oven runs at 2.45 gigahertz, roughly a hundred thousand
times higher in frequency, and by an entirely different mechanism, dielectric heating of water
molecules. The only established biological effect at induction frequencies is the induction of small
currents in body tissue, which at sufficient strength would stimulate nerve and muscle.

The relevant exposure limits are set by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation
Protection, whose 2010 guidelines for time-varying fields specify reference levels precisely to keep
induced tissue currents well below the stimulation threshold with a large safety margin. Measurement
studies of domestic induction hobs, including work commissioned by European regulators, generally
find that at the normal cooking position — a person standing at the front edge, torso perhaps 20 to
30 centimetres from the coil — exposure is within the public reference levels, though at very close
range, essentially pressing the abdomen against the hob edge while a badly matched or offset pan is
running at full boost, some studies have measured values approaching or locally exceeding the
reference level. The reference levels are themselves conservative proxies, and exceeding one is not
the same as exceeding the underlying basic restriction on induced field in tissue. The sensible and
entirely cost-free precaution is to stand a normal arm's length back and to use a correctly sized,
centred pan, which is good practice anyway.

Implanted cardiac devices deserve specific attention. Pacemakers and implantable
cardioverter-defibrillators contain sensing circuitry that can, in principle, misinterpret an external
field as cardiac activity, causing inappropriate inhibition or, rarely, an inappropriate shock.
Studies including a widely cited 2006 investigation in the journal Europace found that interference
was measurable only at very close range and predominantly in unipolar-configured devices with the
patient standing unusually close and using an offset pan. Manufacturers and cardiology bodies
converge on a simple recommendation: keep at least 30 centimetres, and preferably 60, between the
implanted device and an operating hob, do not lean over an active zone, and consult the device
manufacturer and your cardiologist, who can check the device's sensing configuration.

For everyone else, the far more significant health consideration runs the other way. Replacing a gas
burner with induction removes indoor combustion products from the kitchen entirely, and that is a
substantial, well-documented improvement in air quality.

sections.heading: Electrical Supply, Circuits and Installation
sections.body:
Induction concentrates a great deal of electrical power into a small appliance, and the supply is the
practical constraint that most often decides what is possible in a given kitchen.

A full-size four-zone domestic hob typically has a connected load of 7.2 to 11 kilowatts, though most
implement power sharing so that the simultaneous total is capped below the sum of the zones. On a
230-volt single-phase European supply, 7.4 kilowatts draws 32 amperes, which requires a dedicated
radial circuit in 6 square millimetre cable protected at 32 amperes, and in many jurisdictions a
residual current device. Larger hobs are often supplied for two-phase or three-phase connection with
a bridging arrangement selected at the terminal block, and getting that configuration wrong is a
classic installation fault that produces a hob where half the zones do not work.

In North America the situation is more sharply divided. A built-in induction range or cooktop runs on
a 240-volt split-phase circuit, usually 40 or 50 amperes, wired as a dedicated feed to the appliance.
A portable single-zone induction hob plugged into a standard 120-volt, 15-ampere outlet is limited by
the National Electrical Code's 80 per cent continuous-load rule to about 1,440 watts of continuous
draw, which is why almost every portable unit is rated 1,800 watts and cannot sustain that
indefinitely, and why they should never share a circuit with another significant load. This
limitation is real and is the main reason a portable induction plate feels less powerful than a
built-in zone.

Because the supply requirement is the biggest barrier to replacing gas in older housing stock, a
recent development is worth knowing: battery-buffered induction ranges, which contain a lithium
battery charged slowly from an ordinary 120-volt outlet and discharged rapidly to supply full
cooking power. These appeared commercially around 2022 and allow a full induction range to be
installed without upgrading a service panel, at considerable cost.

Physical installation has its own requirements. The hob needs ventilation clearance, generally a gap
at the rear or underside of the cabinet, and must not be installed directly above an oven that lacks
a cooling fan or above a drawer that would block airflow. The cut-out dimensions must be exact
because the glass is supported at the edges. Sealant must be applied so that a boil-over cannot run
into the cabinet and reach the electronics. And the appliance should not be installed over a
dishwasher or fridge unless the manufacturer explicitly permits it, since both generate heat and
humidity.

One further note that catches people out: an induction hob and a downdraught extractor in the same
worktop can interact, and some manufacturers specify a minimum separation. Similarly, running an
induction hob directly beneath a metal extractor canopy at close range is generally fine, but a metal
splashback pressed against the hob edge can, in rare installations, warm noticeably from stray field.

sections.heading: Variants: Portable, Commercial, Wok, All-Metal and Hybrid
sections.body:
The domestic four-zone hob is only one expression of the technology, and the variants illuminate
where the physics gives more room.

Portable single-zone plates are the cheapest entry, typically 1,400 to 2,000 watts, and are extremely
useful as an extra burner, for camping with a generator, in a caravan, for canning where a stable
sustained boil is wanted, and as a way to test whether you like induction before committing. Their
weaknesses are the supply limit, aggressive duty cycling at low settings, and usually a small coil
that suits small pans only.

Commercial induction is a different class of machine. Ranges intended for professional kitchens run
3.5 to 5 kilowatts per zone on three-phase supplies, use half-bridge or full-bridge inverters with
serious cooling, are built to be run at full output for hours, and often carry a probe input for
closed-loop temperature control. Induction woks with concave coils, drop-in single hobs for buffet
service, and induction bains-marie and holding wells are all standard. The appeal in a commercial
setting is as much about the extract-air load and staff comfort as about energy cost.

Flexible or full-surface hobs replace discrete zones with an array of small coils under the whole
glass and use pan detection to energise only those coils a pan is actually covering. This allows a
pan of any shape to be placed anywhere, allows two pans to be treated as one bridged zone for a
griddle or fish kettle, and in the most advanced implementations allows the hob to track a pan as it
is slid across the surface and carry its power setting with it.

All-metal induction is the technically interesting frontier. By running at much higher frequency —
often above 100 kilohertz — and using a different inverter topology to match the very low impedance
of a non-magnetic load, a hob can be made to heat aluminium and copper. Panasonic and a few others
have produced such units. They are less efficient with those materials, more expensive, and generate
more electrical noise, so the technology remains niche, but it does dispose of the claim that
induction fundamentally cannot heat non-ferrous metal.

Hybrid appliances hedge. Some ranges combine induction zones with one radiant or gas burner for
users unwilling to give up a flame or wanting to keep a favourite non-magnetic pan. Some
manufacturers offer induction plus a teppanyaki or griddle plate as a fitted accessory, which is
simply a large ferrous plate designed to couple efficiently.

Industrial induction heating, finally, is the parent technology: it is used for forging billets,
brazing, shrink-fitting bearings, sealing foil caps onto bottles, hardening gear teeth, melting metal
in coreless furnaces, and heating semiconductor crucibles. The kitchen hob is a small, carefully
domesticated example of a very large engineering field.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Error Codes and Troubleshooting
sections.body:
Induction hobs are reliable but their failure modes are unlike those of the appliances they replace,
and a little diagnostic vocabulary saves unnecessary service calls.

The commonest complaint is that a zone does not power up or beeps and stops. In the overwhelming
majority of cases this is pan detection: an unsuitable pan, a pan too small for the zone, a warped
base, or a pan not seated centrally. Confirm with a magnet before assuming a fault. A pan that worked
yesterday and does not today has usually warped, which happens when a pan is heated empty or plunged
hot into cold water.

Sudden power reduction during a long cook is normally the thermal protection working as designed.
Every hob monitors the temperature of its IGBTs and of the glass, and reduces or interrupts output
above a threshold. Common causes are a blocked ventilation path, installation in a sealed cabinet,
ambient heat from an oven below, or simply running several zones at high power in a warm kitchen.
Clearing the airflow generally resolves it. A hob that shuts down within a minute or two of starting
is more suspicious and usually indicates a failed cooling fan or a temperature sensor reading wrongly.

Error codes vary by manufacturer but fall into recognisable families: codes for over-temperature,
codes for supply voltage out of range, codes for a control panel fault where a wet or greasy touch
surface registers a permanent phantom press, and codes for a communication failure between the
control board and a power board. A hob that behaves erratically or beeps continuously with nothing on
it is very often simply wet; drying the touch panel thoroughly resolves a surprising proportion of
apparent faults. Isolating the appliance at the wall for a minute and restoring power clears many
latched conditions.

Genuine hardware failures concentrate in a few components. IGBTs fail, usually short-circuit, and
usually take a fuse with them; this presents as one zone completely dead while others work. The
filter capacitors and the bridge rectifier fail with age and heat. Touch-control boards fail from
moisture ingress. Where a manufacturer supplies parts, these are all economically repairable by a
competent technician, and the coils themselves almost never fail. Where a manufacturer does not
supply parts, and many do not, an otherwise sound hob becomes scrap, which is a real and
under-discussed drawback of the technology compared with a gas burner that can be rebuilt with a
screwdriver.

Cracked glass is terminal for safe use and must not be worked around. A crack allows liquid to reach
mains-voltage electronics and can propagate under thermal stress. Isolate the circuit and stop using
the appliance. Chips at the very edge are sometimes tolerable at the manufacturer's discretion, but
anything crossing a cooking zone is not.

sections.heading: Limits, Trade-Offs and When Induction Is the Wrong Tool
sections.body:
An honest account has to include what induction does badly, because the enthusiasm around it
sometimes outruns the evidence.

The hardest limitation is cookware compatibility, and it is not merely an inconvenience. A cook with
an inherited copper batterie de cuisine, a collection of vintage aluminium, or a beloved
non-magnetic clay or glass vessel cannot use any of it. Interface discs are a poor substitute:
they insert a thermal resistance, waste energy to the air, warp over time, and remove the
responsiveness that is induction's principal virtue. Direct-flame techniques — charring a pepper,
toasting a tortilla, blistering a chilli directly on a burner grate, or the flame-wrapped sides of a
true wok stir-fry — have no induction equivalent at all on a flat zone.

Power interruption is the second limit. An induction hob is a computer with a heater attached; in a
power cut it does nothing, whereas a gas burner can be lit with a match. In regions with unreliable
supply or for emergency preparedness this matters, and a household that has electrified fully should
keep an independent means of heating food and boiling water.

Repairability and lifespan are a genuine trade. A well-maintained gas hob can last thirty years and
be repaired indefinitely; an induction hob's expected service life is typically ten to fifteen years
and it depends on a manufacturer continuing to supply proprietary boards. The embodied energy and
materials of the electronics are non-trivial, and the environmental case for induction rests on
operational efficiency and air quality rather than on longevity.

There are smaller irritations. The ceramic glass is hard and reasonably scratch-resistant but brittle
and intolerant of point impact, so a dropped jar or a heavy pan set down carelessly near an edge can
crack it outright. It shows every mark and requires a specific cream cleaner rather than an abrasive.
Sugar spills must be removed while warm or they can pit the surface. Pans buzz. Cheap hobs pulse at
low power. The touch controls are unusable with wet or greasy fingers and impossible with gloves, and
they are far less accessible for a visually impaired cook than a physical knob with detents, an
accessibility regression that manufacturers have been slow to address.

Set against all that, the case remains strong for most people. The speed is real, the control at both
extremes is better than gas once the low-power implementation is decent, the kitchen is cooler and
the air is cleaner, the surface is far safer around children, and cleaning takes seconds instead of
minutes. The reasonable position is that induction is now the best general-purpose domestic cooking
technology, that it is not universally best, and that the decision should be made with the cookware
inventory, the electrical supply, the availability of repair, and the specific cuisine of the
household all considered rather than on efficiency headlines alone.

guides.safetyNote: An induction hob delivers 1.8 to 3.7 kW into a pan almost instantly and an empty or dry pan can exceed 400 °C in under a minute, igniting oil residue and destroying non-stick coatings, which release irritant fumes above about 260 °C and are lethal to pet birds. Never heat an empty pan, never leave hot oil unattended, and smother an oil fire with a lid or fire blanket — never water. The glass stays hot from conducted heat after the pan is removed; treat any zone as hot until the residual-heat indicator clears. Do not place metal utensils, foil, knives, tins or magnetic-strip cards on an active zone: small metal objects can heat rapidly enough to burn, and cards are erased. People with implanted pacemakers or defibrillators should keep at least 30 cm between the device and an operating hob and follow their cardiologist's advice; the field falls off steeply with distance but manufacturers universally advise this margin. A cracked or chipped glass top must be taken out of service immediately, as a spill reaching the electronics beneath is an electrocution and fire risk. Have fixed installations wired by a qualified electrician on a correctly rated dedicated circuit.
